title: Maharashtra's Varkari
hook: a knock at the door while a son is washing his parents' feet, and a brick tossed out for God to stand on

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maharashtra's Varkari: the wari, the dindis, the road where Vitthal is sung. Which walk did you slow down? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-three.

There's a knock at the door. The young man inside doesn't get up. He's kneeling by his old father and mother, washing their feet, and his hands are busy. The visitor at the door, the story says, is God himself, come all the way from far off to see him. And the young man, without leaving his parents, reaches for the nearest thing, a brick, tosses it out through the doorway, and says: please, stand on this, and wait. I'll be with you when I'm done. That's Pundalik. And that brick is why Vitthal stands the way he does.
screen: `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR.` → `A SON WASHING HIS PARENTS' FEET.` → `A BRICK TOSSED OUT.`

segments.voice: Varkaris tell it like this. Pundalik, in some tellings, wasn't always a good son. He had neglected his parents, until something turned him around, and from then on he served them with his whole heart. That service is what draws God to Pandharpur. Krishna, the story says, comes looking for him, because a devotion like that is worth the journey. So God arrives, and Pundalik makes him wait. Stop on that for a moment. A listener might expect that when God comes, everything else is dropped. Here, the son finishes caring for his parents first, and the god of the story doesn't mind. He steps onto the brick, puts his hands on his hips, and waits. That's the shape of Vitthal's image at Pandharpur: standing on a brick, hands on hips, patient. Varkaris say he's still standing there, still waiting, for Pundalik and for everyone who comes after. Now turn the story one more way. What is it saying about where God is found? Not only at a shrine. In a basin of water and two tired old pairs of feet. Pundalik doesn't choose between serving his parents and loving God. To him the serving is the loving, and God agrees by waiting. And one last turn. Look at what the god of this story chooses to do with his power. He stands. He's patient. The Varkari road ends at a god whose whole posture says: take your time, I'm here.
screen: `PUNDALIK SERVES HIS PARENTS` · `GOD ARRIVES, AND WAITS` · `STANDING ON A BRICK, HANDS ON HIPS` · `THE SERVING IS THE LOVING`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone you look after, or someone who once looked after you: their hands, their feet, the way they move when they're tired. Picture yourself doing one small thing for them, like setting down a glass of water or helping with a coat. Stay with it, slowly, without rushing to the next thing. If you pray, you can let that small act be your prayer, the way it was for Pundalik. The bell holds the time.
Maharashtra's Varkari. The tradition whose god stands on Pundalik's brick at Pandharpur, hands on hips, still waiting. Today's word.
Your line: Maharashtra's Varkari. Today, finish one act of care all the way through before you answer the next thing calling for you. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Varkaris retell the story of Pundalik, and pilgrims at Pandharpur visit his shrine as well as Vitthal's, the god who stands on a brick with hands on hips.

trapdoor: what you thought: a brick is just a brick.

notes: Pundalik's story is told as tradition; tellings differ on his earlier neglect of his parents and on whether the visitor is named as Krishna or Vishnu. Confirm the framing.
'Some hear the name Vitthal itself in the brick': popular reading linking Vitthal with vit (brick) is a contested etymology; kept as 'a reading tradition gives'. A Keeper may prefer to cut it.
